hero.h1: Design system services that keep every product consistent
hero.sub: Development-ready component libraries, design tokens, and documentation so teams ship consistent UI without waiting on designers.

summary: Component libraries, tokens, and documentation that scale across teams.
sourceContext: US UI/UX design agency; this page sells the design system engagement (tokens, components, governance) to product organisations whose UI has drifted across teams.
abstract: Design system services build a shared set of design tokens, a development-ready component library and usage documentation so every product team ships a consistent user interface (UI). Our design system engagement takes 8–16 weeks, costs $60,000–$180,000, and ends with a Figma library, tokens in code and a governance model.

sections.answer: A design system is a single source of truth for a product's user interface: design tokens, reusable components, usage guidelines and the governance rules that keep them current. Designers use the Figma library and engineers use the matching coded components, so both teams build from the same parts.
sections.body: A design system differs from a style guide in one way: a style guide documents colours and type, while a design system also ships working components and a process for changing the components. Our design system services follow Atomic Design, from tokens to atoms, molecules and templates, and include the component states defined by an interaction design agency.

sections.h2: What does a design system include?
sections.answer: Our design system services include 6 deliverables: a UI inventory, design tokens, a Figma component library, a coded component library, design system documentation and a governance model.

items.title: UI inventory.
items.body: Every existing screen is captured and grouped, for example duplicate button styles, colour values and spacing values.

items.title: Design tokens.
items.body: Colour, typography, spacing, radius and motion values are stored as tokens in the Design Tokens Community Group (DTCG) format, for example color.text.primary.

items.title: Figma component library.
items.body: Components use variants, auto layout and variables, for example buttons, inputs, modals and data tables.

items.title: Coded component library.
items.body: Components are built with the client's engineers and documented in Storybook, for example with visual regression tests in Chromatic.

items.title: Design system documentation.
items.body: Each component page in Zeroheight or Storybook lists anatomy, states and accessibility rules, for example the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2 contrast ratio of 4.5:1 for body text.

items.title: Governance model.
items.body: A contribution process defines who proposes, reviews and releases changes, for example a monthly release with semantic versioning.

sections.h2: How does the design system process work?
sections.answer: The design system process takes 8–16 weeks (40–80 working days) and runs in 5 steps, from UI inventory to governance handover.

items.title: UI inventory and audit (5–10 days)
items.body: We collect every screen, list duplicate patterns and agree the products and platforms in scope.

items.title: Design tokens and foundations (5–10 days)
items.body: Designers define colour, typography, spacing and elevation tokens, managed in Tokens Studio and exported to code with Style Dictionary.

items.title: Component design (15–30 days)
items.body: Designers build each component in Figma with variants and states, starting with the most used components, for example buttons, inputs and navigation.

items.title: Code alignment and documentation (10–20 days)
items.body: Engineers match each Figma component to code in Storybook, and designers write usage guidelines and accessibility rules per component.

items.title: Governance and rollout (5–10 days)
items.body: We set up design system governance, train product teams in 2 workshops and release version 1.0 of the design system.

sections.h2: What are the benefits of a design system?
sections.answer: A design system has 4 benefits: it increases component reuse rate, improves UI consistency, reduces design and development time and develops design maturity.

items.title: Increases component reuse rate
items.body: Teams pick existing components from the Figma and Storybook libraries instead of building new ones, which increases the share of screens built from shared parts.

items.title: Improves UI consistency
items.body: Shared tokens and components improve consistency of colour, spacing and behaviour across every product, platform and team.

items.title: Reduces design and development time
items.body: Designers assemble screens from ready components and engineers reuse tested code, which reduces the time from design to release.

items.title: Develops design maturity
items.body: The governance model develops a shared design practice, with product teams contributing components through one review process.

sections.answer: A design system includes tokens, components, code, documentation and governance; a UI kit includes only the visual components in a design file. Teams with 1 product and 1 designer start with a UI kit, and teams with several products need a design system.

sections.h2: How much does a design system cost?
sections.answer: A design system costs $60,000–$180,000 and takes 8–16 weeks. The price depends on 4 factors: the number of components, the number of platforms, the number of brands or themes and the depth of code alignment.
sections.body: A single-brand web design system with 25–30 components, a Figma library and Storybook documentation sits near $60,000. A multi-brand design system with light and dark themes, 60–80 web and mobile components and a governance rollout sits near $180,000. Teams that maintain the design system after release book an embedded user experience (UX) design team for $15,000–$40,000 per month through UX consulting services.

sections.h2: When does a growing product team need design system services?
sections.answer: A growing product team needs design system services in 5 situations:
items: The same component exists in several versions, if each team designed its own buttons and forms.
A rebrand is planned, if colours and typography are hard-coded across products.
Design-to-development handoff takes weeks, if engineers rebuild each screen from scratch.
A second product or platform launches, if the new team needs the existing UI patterns.
Accessibility fixes repeat on every screen, if no shared component holds the contrast and focus rules.

sections.answer: These answers cover the 5 questions buyers ask most about design system services.

faqs.q: Does a design system include code?
faqs.a: Yes. Our design system includes coded components documented in Storybook, built with the client's engineers to match the Figma library 1:1.

faqs.q: Can a design system work with an existing product?
faqs.a: Yes. A design system for an existing product starts with a UI inventory and replaces duplicate patterns screen by screen, without a full redesign.

faqs.q: Which tools does a design system use?
faqs.a: A design system uses Figma for the design library, Tokens Studio and Style Dictionary for design tokens, and Storybook for coded components.

faqs.q: Should a startup build a design system?
faqs.a: No. A startup with 1 product and 1–2 designers needs a UI kit and design tokens first; a full design system fits when 2 or more teams build on the same product.

faqs.q: How long does a design system take?
faqs.a: A design system takes 8–16 weeks, which equals 40–80 working days, from UI inventory to the version 1.0 release.
